heading: PROPHET ILYĀS (AS)
title: THE COURAGE TO WORSHIP ALLAH ALONE
themes: Tawḥīd • Taqwā • Sincere Counsel • Steadfastness • Integrity • Good Deeds • Humility
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 11 SELECTED QUR’ANIC VERSES
introduction: Volume Eighteen follows the previous world on Prophet Sulaymān (AS). The Qur’an explicitly describes Ilyās (AS) as one of the messengers, records his call to his people to fear Allah and leave the worship of Baʿl, and states that his people denied him. It also records an exception for sincere servants, honourable remembrance, peace upon him, and Allah’s praise of him as a believing servant (al-Ṣāffāt 37:123–132). Al-Anʿām 6:85 names him among the righteous. These are the firmly attested historical teaching points of this volume.

Because the Qur’anic account is concise, our narrative does not invent additional episodes about his childhood, parents, residence, journeys, date of birth, specific punishments, death or supposed miracles. Eight modern fictional episodes instead show Imaan, Akhlaq and their community preparing a “What Deserves Our Loyalty?” exhibition. These scenes are never presented as events in the lifetime of Ilyās (AS).

stories.title: The Next Card in the Library
stories.subtitle: A short account can hold a great lesson

blocks.text: The blue promise folder from the previous exhibition was overflowing. There were maps, cards, tiny paper leaves and Akhlaq’s handwritten reminder: “A blessing is a responsibility.” He had expected their next Prophet’s story to require another enormous display. Instead, Dadi Jaan placed one slender bookmark on the table. On it were two references: al-Ṣāffāt 37:123–132 and al-Anʿām 6:85. “Only these?” Akhlaq asked. “The Qur’an speaks concisely about Prophet Ilyās,” Dadi answered. “Being concise does not make a lesson small.” Imaan noticed several printed stories tucked into Akhlaq’s notebook. They described long journeys, strange encounters and dramatic scenes. “Did the Qur’an tell all of these?” she asked. Akhlaq hesitated. He had saved the pages because they sounded exciting. Sheikh Uncle opened the verses and showed them what was established: Ilyās was a messenger; he called his people to taqwā and worship of Allah; many denied him; Allah praised him. “Our first responsibility,” he said, “is not to improve the story by inventing details.” At school, Sir Zameer announced the new exhibition theme: WHAT DESERVES OUR LOYALTY? Akhlaq wanted a large poster that said EVERY DETAIL ABOUT ILYĀS. Imaan crossed out “every detail” and wrote WHAT ALLAH TELLS US ABOUT ILYĀS. It looked less dramatic, but it was truthful. That afternoon Akhlaq carefully removed the unverified pages and placed them in a folder marked “Needs checking.” The exhibition had begun before anyone had made a poster. They had already learned to value evidence above excitement.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Respect a Qur’anic account by separating established teaching from unverified stories.

At the academy entrance, a blank board carried a question: “What matters most?” Children answered in many ways. Mohsin wrote “winning the annual trophy”; Mohsina wrote “helping people”; Akhlaq wrote “being noticed.” Imaan looked at the different answers. “Are these all things we worship?” she asked. Sir Zameer explained that admiring an achievement and worshipping it are not the same. Worship, duʿāʾ and ultimate devotion belong to Allah alone. He opened Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt and read the passage about Prophet Ilyās. Ilyās asked his people why they called upon Baʿl and turned away from Allah, their Lord and the Lord of their forefathers. “So the message was not simply ‘be nice’?” Akhlaq asked. “Correct,” replied the teacher. “Its centre is Tawḥīd. Our manners and good deeds must grow from devotion to Allah.” A student offered to draw a large picture of the false object mentioned in the verse. Sir Zameer declined. “We do not need to make an attraction out of false worship. A carefully written reference is enough.” Instead the children made a circle of cards naming good actions: prayer, honesty, gratitude and service. At the centre they placed the words WORSHIP ALLAH ALONE. Akhlaq moved his “being noticed” card away from the middle. “Being noticed can feel important,” he admitted. “But it should not decide everything I do.” They left the board in the hallway so families could read and discuss it. The board was quieter than a competition. It asked a much greater question.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Let love and worship of Allah guide actions rather than popularity.

stories.title: The Rule Everyone Followed
stories.subtitle: Popularity cannot turn a wrong action into a right one

blocks.text: A new game became popular during recess: the oldest pupils hid a younger pupil’s water bottle, then returned it only after everyone had laughed. Some called it a harmless tradition. When Akhlaq’s friends invited him to join, he wondered whether refusing would make him seem disloyal. “Everyone does it,” one boy told him. Akhlaq remembered the exhibition board. Prophet Ilyās had reminded his people of Allah, even while the false practice around them was familiar. Akhlaq understood that the classroom prank was not equivalent to worshipping Baʿl. Yet a limited lesson was useful: the fact that a group approves of something does not make it good. He said he would not hide the bottle. “It worries the younger children,” he explained. His friends teased him for being too serious. Akhlaq felt his face grow warm. Instead of arguing, he moved towards the teacher on duty and told him what was happening. The teacher brought the group together and asked how the younger pupils had felt. One child said she had spent lunch thinking her bottle had been stolen. The boys apologised and agreed to play a different game. Later, Imaan asked Akhlaq whether he had been frightened. “A little,” he admitted. “Was that wrong?” “No,” she replied. “It is possible to feel nervous and still choose wisely.” At home, Salaam praised him for seeking adult help rather than confronting the group alone. Akhlaq wrote a second phrase for the exhibition: A CROWD IS NOT THE MEASURE OF RIGHT AND WRONG.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Refuse an unkind practice and seek safe support when group pressure grows.

The class charity box was supposed to collect unused pencils and notebooks for pupils who needed them. At the end of the week, Imaan noticed that several usable notebooks had been thrown away because their covers were untidy. Mohsin shrugged. “They look old. Nobody will want them.” Imaan wanted to protest in front of everyone. But she remembered how quickly embarrassment can turn a useful correction into a quarrel. She asked Sir Zameer whether they could check the donation rules together. They discovered that clean, partly used notebooks were welcome when the remaining pages were separated and prepared properly. Imaan approached the team calmly. “We might be wasting things that could help someone,” she said. One classmate rolled his eyes. “You always find a problem.” The comment hurt. Imaan did not pretend it was pleasant, nor did she accuse the whole team of wrongdoing. She showed the written instructions and offered to sort the notebooks herself. Mohsina joined her. Soon the others helped too. In the afternoon, Sheikh Uncle explained that Prophet Ilyās (AS) was rejected by his people when he called them to the truth. The Qur’an does not provide a diary of his emotions or every meeting he held; it provides the message and the response. Their classroom issue was far smaller and unrelated to the sacred historical event. Still, it helped the children consider how to remain honest without becoming cruel. Imaan’s final note read: GOOD ADVICE NEEDS TRUTH, CARE AND THE RIGHT MOMENT.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Offer accurate advice calmly, and do not invent accusations when a suggestion is rejected.

stories.title: The Quiet Corner of the Exhibition
stories.subtitle: Sincerity need not seek a crowd

blocks.text: By Monday the exhibition preparations had become a competition. Team Amanah had been assigned a corner near the back wall. Akhlaq complained that visitors would never notice it. Mohsina preferred the quieter space. “People will be able to read without being pushed,” she said. The team planned a small source-check station: children would match statements to the actual verses about Ilyās. One card stated that the Qur’an calls him a messenger. Another claimed the Qur’an describes exactly where he lived. A third quoted Allah’s praise of him as a believing servant. The children could mark each as “stated in the source” or “not established by this source.” When the first visitors arrived, Akhlaq watched the crowded entrance and wondered whether their station was a failure. Then a younger pupil came over, puzzled by a story he had heard. Imaan helped him find the correct verse. Mohsin explained why a detail could remain unverified without insulting the person who had repeated it. The boy smiled and asked to take the source card home. Later, Dadi Jaan visited. “How many prizes did you win?” she asked. “None yet,” Akhlaq replied. “But a child learned something true.” Dadi nodded. “That is not a small result.” She pointed to Qur’an 37:128, where an exception is made for devoted servants of Allah. “We cannot measure people’s sincerity from a school booth,” she said. “But we can choose work that serves others, even if applause is quiet.” Akhlaq took down the sign that had promised “the most exciting station” and replaced it with “read, check, understand.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Choose useful work for the right reasons, without demanding praise.

stories.title: The Prize That Changed the Rules
stories.subtitle: Good deeds remain good without trophies

blocks.text: The academy announced a prize for the best educational display. Akhlaq immediately counted their cards and added a shiny border to the table. But the group discovered that one source card was wrong. It claimed a detail about Prophet Ilyās that did not appear in their verified references. Removing it would leave a noticeable empty space just before judging. “We could leave it,” suggested a teammate. “It sounds convincing.” Mohsina shook her head. “We would be teaching something we have not checked.” Akhlaq stared at the empty space. He wanted the prize, but he knew what the exhibition was supposed to teach. They removed the card, wrote a small correction and placed a question mark where the unsupported statement had stood. The judges asked why their display had a gap. Imaan explained the correction without blaming anybody. “We are still checking that detail, so we chose not to present it as established.” One judge thanked them for being careful. The class did not receive the largest trophy. Instead, the teacher praised the group’s transparency during the closing gathering. Akhlaq was disappointed for a moment, then felt lighter. The value of the work had not disappeared with the trophy. When Sheikh Uncle read Qur’an 37:131 about Allah rewarding doers of good, he reminded the children that the verse does not mean every sincere action will earn a worldly award. The children could not award themselves Allah’s reward. They could, however, act truthfully and be grateful for an opportunity to do good.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Never sacrifice the truth to make an achievement look impressive.

stories.title: The Name That Remained
stories.subtitle: A legacy can be an invitation to good

blocks.text: On the final afternoon, the classes created a memory wall for people who had helped the academy. Names were written on leaves, each accompanied by an actual service: repairing a shelf, mentoring a younger pupil, making the library accessible, checking a source carefully. Akhlaq suggested adding the names of the most popular pupils at the top. Dadi Jaan asked what the wall was meant to honour. “Helpful actions,” he admitted. “Then let the descriptions show the actions,” she replied. Sheikh Uncle opened the Qur’an to the words about honourable remembrance and peace upon Ilyās (37:129–130). Allah preserved this praise of His messenger. “We are not comparing school appreciation with Allah’s honour of a Prophet,” he said. “We can only learn a smaller ethical lesson: your reputation should not be built on boasting.” The children revised the wall. Some of the most important contributions were those nobody had noticed until now. A quiet student had spent weeks keeping the reading corner tidy. Another had translated instructions for a newcomer. The wall brought their service into view without ranking their hearts. Imaan added a final card to the Prophet’s source station: THE QUR’AN PRAISES ILYĀS AS A BELIEVING SERVANT. Akhlaq read it carefully. “So we remember him because Allah honoured him,” he said, “not because we imagined his story would make an exciting competition.” The evening ended with modest conversation rather than a grand contest. The wall remained on display for the next group of students.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour genuine service without making popularity the measure of worth.

stories.title: The Card Worth Keeping
stories.subtitle: Faith and conduct must travel together

blocks.text: Dadi Jaan gathered the family around the table after the exhibition. The old compass was still beside their family tree, where it had remained through several volumes of learning. Imaan placed eleven source cards in order. Ten came from Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt and one from Sūrat al-Anʿām. Akhlaq read the themes aloud: a messenger, a call to taqwā, worship of Allah alone, rejection of the message, the devoted servants, Allah’s honour, good deeds and faith. “The Qur’an says all this without telling us every moment of his life,” he observed. Salaam nodded. “A faithful account is enough. We must not fill every silence with fiction.” The children reviewed their week. They had refused an unkind prank, checked a source, given calm advice and prepared useful notes. None of those events had happened to Prophet Ilyās. They were modern opportunities to practise modest lessons drawn from the Qur’anic guidance. Salamah asked each person to choose one action for the next seven days. Mohsin chose to be fair when his friends disagreed. Mohsina chose to correct mistakes without embarrassing people. Imaan chose to check what she heard before repeating it. Akhlaq chose to remember prayer even when busy. Dadi smiled. “And if one day you forget?” “We try again,” he said. On the final blank card he wrote: WORSHIP ALLAH. SEEK TRUTH. DO GOOD. The compass did not glow. There was no hidden gate. Its quiet needle reminded them that direction matters more than drama. A new learning world would soon begin, but this lesson was ready to travel with them.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Let Tawḥīd guide honest, useful action beyond the lesson screen.

review.meaning: Ilyās was certainly one of Allah’s messengers.
He asked his people whether they would not have taqwā.
He questioned their calling upon Baʿl while leaving the Best of creators.
Allah is your Lord and the Lord of your earliest forefathers.
They denied him, and the verse warns of their being brought forth.
An exception is made for Allah’s devoted servants.
Allah preserved honourable remembrance of him among later generations.
Peace is pronounced upon Ilyās (with the Qur’anic form to be explained).
Allah thus rewards those who do good.
He was among Allah’s believing servants.

synthesis.text: What the Qur’an teaches about Ilyās (AS)

The Qur’an names Ilyās as one of Allah’s messengers and among the righteous. It records his call to his people: have taqwā and leave the worship of Baʿl in favour of Allah, their Lord and the Lord of their forefathers. Many denied his message. The Qur’an also mentions Allah’s devoted servants and preserves a blessed remembrance of Ilyās, greeting him with peace and praising him among the believing servants. The Qur’an does not provide a full chronology of his personal life. We must honour the evidence without inventing a dramatic biography.
Eight lessons to carry forward
Worship belongs to Allah alone.
Use reliable Qur’anic evidence when learning about Prophets.
Do not follow a harmful practice only because it is common.
Speak truth with care; harshness does not make an argument better.
Seek trustworthy adult support when a group pressures you.
Continue doing right even if the response is not immediate applause.
Appreciate genuine service without pretending to know another person’s heart.
Let remembrance of Allah lead to honesty, helpfulness and gratitude.
Seven-day character practice
Day
Voluntary daily action
Private reflection
Read or listen to a reviewed verse about Ilyās with an adult
What is established by the verse?
Complete an entrusted household or school duty
Did I fulfil my responsibility?
Respectfully decline an unkind joke
Did I choose safety and kindness?
Ask for the source of a doubtful religious claim
Could I admit uncertainty?
Give advice kindly when appropriate
Was my tone respectful?
Thank a person for their genuine help
Did I avoid flattery?
Choose one small ongoing good deed
What will I continue?
Family reflection and learning checks

Ask without pressuring children: “Why did Ilyās call his people to Allah?” “Which details does the Qur’an actually give?” “How do we refuse something unkind safely?” “What if we try a good action and nobody notices?” “How can one small act improve our home?” Answers are not confessions or spiritual scores.

Knowledge assessment: identify Ilyās; locate al-Ṣāffāt 37:123–132; recognise Baʿl as the false object mentioned in the passage; identify Tawḥīd; mark invented biography as unsupported. Ethical assessment: choose a respectful, safe decision and explain it in age-appropriate language.
Private Muḥāsabah: Practised / Still learning / Skip. Do not score sincerity, sadness, belief, parental relationships or personal distress.
Final carry-forward

Imaan and Akhlaq leave this world with three sentences: Worship Allah alone. Tell the truth responsibly. Do useful good even when applause is quiet. Their next volume will introduce a new Prophet through verified evidence, not through an invented dramatic cliffhanger.
